title: Founder's bookshelf
note: Five books reduced to their working models, each idea credited: Good Strategy Bad Strategy (Richard Rumelt), High Output Management (Andrew S. Grove), The Effective Executive (Peter F. Drucker), Scaling People (Claire Hughes Johnson) and The Ideal Team Player (Patrick Lencioni). Built from published summaries, not the books' text. Ready, Fire, Aim was dropped: its speed-over-perfection idea lives in Go-to-market.

concepts.s: Five books reduce to four loops an operator runs: set strategy, multiply output through others, manage your own effectiveness, and run the company on written norms.

x.b:
• Strategy (Rumelt): diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent actions.
  • Output (Grove): a manager's output is the output of the teams they run or influence, so pick high-leverage activities.
  • Effectiveness (Drucker): time, contribution, strengths, concentration, decisions.
  • Operating system (Hughes Johnson, Lencioni): written founding documents, a cadence, structured hiring and honest performance management.

None of these books rests on controlled studies; they earn their place on leverage per word.
Trap: Collecting frameworks instead of running one loop well. Pick the loop where you are weakest this quarter.
Missed quarter: check strategy first (was there a diagnosis?), then output (were your hours high leverage?), then the operating system (did anyone own the metric?).

cards.q: A quarter was missed. Which loop do you check first, and what is the question?
cards.a: Strategy: was there a real diagnosis and a focused guiding policy?

cards.q: What is the evidence base for these management books?
cards.a: Practitioner experience, not controlled studies; they are kept for leverage per word.

concepts.s: Rumelt: a strategy is a diagnosis of the critical challenge, a guiding policy for meeting it, and coherent actions that carry it out; anything else is goals or fluff.

x.b:
• Diagnosis: what is going on and which one or two factors matter most.
  • Guiding policy: the approach; it rules most options out.
  • Coherent actions: coordinated resource commitments that reinforce each other.

Rumelt's four hallmarks of bad strategy: fluff, failure to face the challenge, mistaking goals for strategy, and bad strategic objectives (a long list, or goals as hard as the original problem).
Trap: "Grow revenue 30%" is a goal, not a strategy. It names no obstacle and no approach.
Diagnosis: we are spread across five segments and win none. Policy: own dental offices in three states. Actions: one integration, one association partnership, a sales hire who knows the trade.
Which options does your guiding policy rule out? If none, it is not a policy.

cards.q: A plan lists twelve objectives and a revenue target. Which two hallmarks of bad strategy are these?
cards.a: Mistaking goals for strategy, plus bad strategic objectives (a long, unfocused list).

cards.q: How do you test whether a guiding policy is real?
cards.a: It must rule out most options and point at the obstacle named in the diagnosis.

concepts.s: Grove: a manager's output is the output of the teams they run or influence, so spend your hours on the activities with the highest leverage on that output.

x.b:
Output = sum of (each activity x its leverage). High leverage: an activity that affects many people or a long time (training, setting goals, a key decision), or where your unique knowledge changes the result. Negative leverage: meddling, slow decisions that stall a team.

Grove treats training as core manager work, and meetings as the medium of management.

Trap: Measuring yourself by personal tasks done. A manager's busiest day can be their lowest-output day.
Trap: Delegating without monitoring. Grove's delegation still checks in, at a frequency set by the person's maturity on the task.
Choosing between fixing a dashboard yourself (2 hours, one output) and teaching two analysts the pattern (3 hours, every future dashboard): the second has far higher leverage.

cards.q: You spent the day closing tickets yourself while three reports waited on a decision. What did Grove's lens miss?
cards.a: Negative leverage: your delay stalled the team's output, which is your real output.

cards.q: Why does Grove call training high leverage?
cards.a: A few hours of your time raises the output of each trained person on every future task.

concepts.s: Grove: run work like a production line: watch leading indicators, pair each measure with its counter-measure, and catch problems at the lowest-value stage.

x.b:
• Black box: put windows on a process with indicators that warn before the output arrives (leading, trend, linearity).
  • Paired indicators: measuring something distorts it, so pair it with its counter-effect: speed with defects, inventory with shortages.
  • Limiting step: build the schedule backward from the slowest, costliest step.
  • Lowest-value stage: catch defects before more value is added to them.
Trap: A single metric becomes the target and gets gamed. Always ask what its pair is.
Data team KPI: pipelines shipped per sprint. Pair it with incidents per pipeline. Add tests at ingestion (lowest-value stage) rather than at the dashboard.

cards.q: Your team is rewarded for tickets closed per week. What should you pair it with?
cards.a: A quality counter-measure such as reopened tickets or defects, so speed isn't bought with errors.

cards.q: Where should a data quality check go, per Grove's production principles?
cards.a: At the earliest, lowest-value stage (ingestion), before more work is built on bad data.

concepts.s: Grove: match how closely you manage to a person's maturity on this specific task, from structured direction when it is new to light monitoring when mastered.

x.b:
• Low task-relevant maturity: structured, task-oriented: what, when, how.
  • Medium: individual, two-way, focused on support and reasoning.
  • High: agree on objectives, then monitor lightly.

Maturity is per task, not per person, and you always monitor. One-on-ones, owned by the report, are the main tool; meet more often when maturity is low.

Trap: Hands-off with a senior person on an unfamiliar task. Seniority is not task-relevant maturity.
Trap: Micromanaging a master. It wastes your leverage and their motivation.
Your best SQL engineer takes on their first vendor negotiation: weekly check-ins and a shared plan, even though you never review their SQL.

cards.q: A strong engineer leads their first migration. What style does Grove prescribe?
cards.a: Closer, more structured management for that task, because maturity is task-specific.

cards.q: Who should own the agenda of a Grove one-on-one?
cards.a: The report; the manager listens, asks and coaches.

concepts.s: Drucker: record where your time actually goes, cut what wastes it, consolidate the rest into large blocks, and do first things first, one at a time.

x.b:
1. Record time as you spend it for 3-4 weeks, twice a year; memory lies.
  2. Prune: what if this were not done at all? Who else could do it? What of mine wastes your time?
  3. Consolidate: important work needs long, uninterrupted blocks.
  4. Concentrate: one priority at a time; drop an old activity before adding a new one. Posteriorities (what not to do) are the hard part.

Trap: Letting pressures set priorities. Drucker's test: who decides, you or the inbox?
Trap: Recurring crises. A crisis that repeats should be foreseen and made routine.
A week's log shows 40% in meetings and no block over 45 minutes. Cut two standing meetings and protect two mornings a week for the migration design.

cards.q: Why record time as it is spent rather than estimate it?
cards.a: Memory of how time was spent is unreliable; only a live log shows the real allocation.

cards.q: You want to start a new initiative. What does Drucker require first?
cards.a: Drop an existing activity (slough off yesterday) so the new one gets concentrated effort.

concepts.s: Drucker: ask what you can contribute that changes results, judge yourself by output, and staff for what people do uncommonly well while making their weaknesses irrelevant.

x.b:
Anyone responsible for a contribution that affects results is an executive, manager or not. Redefine your contribution in every new job, and ask who uses your output.

Staffing: start from what a person does uncommonly well; design jobs by task, not personality; accept weaknesses to get strengths, never a lack of integrity. A job that defeats two or three good people in a row is badly designed.

Trap: Hiring for the absence of weakness. You get mediocrity.
Trap: Trying to reform your boss. Make their strengths productive instead.
A brilliant modeler is weak at stakeholder updates. Pair them with a strong communicator rather than spending a year fixing the weakness.

cards.q: A role has burned out three capable people in a row. What does Drucker conclude?
cards.a: The job is badly designed; redesign it rather than hiring a fourth person.

cards.q: What weakness does Drucker say you never accept for the sake of a strength?
cards.a: A lack of integrity.

concepts.s: Drucker: make few, fundamental decisions: classify the problem, define what the decision must achieve, start from opinions, demand dissent, and build in action and feedback.

x.b:
1. Classify: generic problems get a rule; true exceptions get a one-off decision.
  2. Boundary conditions: what it must achieve.
  3. What's right before what's acceptable.
  4. Build in action: who must know and who acts.
  5. Feedback: check against events; go and look.

Start from opinions treated as hypotheses; no decision without disagreement. Decide only when acting beats waiting; never half-act.
Trap: Treating a generic problem as a string of unique events. You keep firefighting what a policy would end.
Third ad-hoc data-access exception this month: it is generic. Write an access policy instead of approving the fourth.

cards.q: Everyone agrees on a big decision in five minutes. What would Drucker do?
cards.a: Hold the decision until real dissent and alternatives surface; unanimity means it isn't understood yet.

cards.q: The same kind of exception keeps landing on your desk. What is the fix?
cards.a: Classify it as generic and set a rule or policy.

concepts.s: Hughes Johnson: write down the mission, goals and values, then run the company on a visible operating system of strategy, metrics, owners and cadence.

x.b:
• Founding documents: a specific mission, concrete long-term goals, values used in hiring and reviews, and a charter per team. Write them once there is traction; past about 40-50 people they become the touchstones.
  • Operating system: strategy as resource allocation (it should hurt), metrics at each level, clear owners, weekly team reviews, quarterly business reviews, a steady cadence.

Trap: Restructuring reactively or around individuals. Align structure to strategy.
Trap: A cadence nobody revisits. Keep the rhythm, but change it when the plan changes.
A 30-person startup with traction writes its mission and three values now, and adds team charters and quarterly reviews as it nears 50.

cards.q: When should a startup write its founding documents, per Hughes Johnson?
cards.a: Once it has traction; past about 40-50 people they become the shared touchstones.

cards.q: A strategy funds every team's wish list. What is missing?
cards.a: Real resource allocation: a strategy should hurt by saying no.

concepts.s: Hire through a structured process aimed at specific traits (Lencioni's humble, hungry and people-smart are a useful lens) and never lower the bar to fill a seat.

x.b:
Hughes Johnson: treat recruiting like sales (pipeline ahead of need), honest job descriptions, one rubric, several trained interviewers, the hiring manager decides, fix mistakes fast.

Lencioni: humble (credit to others), hungry (self-driven), smart (reads people). The hardest to spot is hungry plus smart without humility: the skillful politician. It is a lens from a fable, with no outcome data.
Trap: Unstructured "culture fit" interviews. They reward similarity, not the traits you need.
Ask how they treated the coordinator who scheduled them, and for a mistake they owned. Listen for "we" over "I".

cards.q: Which Lencioni archetype is hardest to spot in interviews?
cards.a: The skillful politician: hungry and smart but not humble.

cards.q: The pipeline is thin and a seat has been open two months. What does the rule say?
cards.a: Don't lower the bar; build the pipeline ahead of need instead.

concepts.s: Hughes Johnson: give feedback continuously as tested hypotheses, run fair, calibrated reviews, and act decisively on both high and low performers.

x.b:
• Continuous: observe across situations, form a hypothesis, test it in conversation, say it before you feel ready.
  • Reviews: announce criteria in advance; self, peer and manager inputs; calibrate across managers for bias; pay by a written philosophy.
  • Act: stretch and recognize high performers; low performers get documented conversations, then a plan or a respectful exit.
Trap: Saving feedback for the annual review. Surprises in a review mean the manager failed earlier.
"I've noticed in the last three reviews you let the client set the scope. My hypothesis: you avoid saying no. Does that match?"

cards.q: An employee is surprised by a low rating at review time. Whose failure is it?
cards.a: The manager's: feedback should have been continuous, so the review holds no surprises.

cards.q: How does Hughes Johnson frame difficult feedback?
cards.a: As a hypothesis built from repeated observations, tested in conversation.
